routes.description: Establish that humans are personally accountable under a trustworthy divine moral order, that judgment answers genuine guilt, and that Christ's substitutionary death and resurrection make merciful salvation coherent through repentance and faith.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine authority and human culpability are adequately grounded, punishment and substitution are shown to be morally intelligible, and repentance, faith, grace, and resurrection form a coherent account of salvation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the account of sin, judgment, atonement, and salvation into a morally and explanatorily coherent gospel.

centralBridges.description: Ground God's moral authority and show that human beings bear personal guilt for their own wrongdoing.
Explain why judgment is deserved and how Christ's substitution permits mercy without abandoning justice.
Specify how repentance, faith, grace, resurrection, and personal transformation provide salvation rather than moral works.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply a warrant for trusting God, scripture, creation, conscience, and claimed transformative experience.
Reconcile divine foreknowledge and a fallen creation with individual responsibility and confidence in divine justice.

routes.description: Show that the gospel account fails moral or explanatory scrutiny because responsibility is misassigned, substitution does not resolve wrongdoing, divine alternatives appear less harmful, and its foundational and salvific claims lack reliable evidential support.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if central features of guilt, judgment, atonement, or salvation are shown to be unjustified, internally unstable, needlessly designed, or dependent on methods that cannot reliably establish their truth.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that the proposed account of sin, atonement, and salvation does not jointly satisfy moral and explanatory standards.

centralBridges.description: Test whether inherited guilt and an omniscient creator's choices are compatible with personal culpability and just punishment.
Test whether sacrificial substitution is necessary, morally permissible, and capable of addressing defective character or repeated wrongdoing.
Require non-circular, discriminating support for God, scripture, resurrection, and the claimed operation of salvation.
Compare the gospel's history of suffering, hiddenness, judgment, and rescue with less harmful divine alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Determine whether conversion and salvation claims permit adverse experience to count against them.
Distinguish evidence-proportioned confidence from faith, assertion, assumed design, and appeals to humility.

sections.title: Human Guilt, Divine Foreknowledge, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: The justice of sin and judgment depends on whether people are accountable for their conduct despite inherited conditions, divine foreknowledge, creative choice, and the availability of alternative worlds.

sections.title: Substitutionary Atonement, Forgiveness, and Moral Repair
sections.rationale: This issue directly tests whether Christ's sacrifice is necessary and just, whether penalty payment can ground forgiveness, and whether substitution addresses the wrongdoer's underlying moral condition.

sections.title: Evidence for God, Scripture, and Resurrection
sections.rationale: The gospel's explanation requires support for its divine lawgiver, scriptural authority, and resurrection claims, making the dispute over creation, revelation, faith, and evidential standards structurally central.

sections.title: Repentance, Faith, Conversion, and the Salvation Promise
sections.rationale: The account must explain how salvation is obtained and known while addressing whether failed conversion, continued nonbelief, or contrary experience can meaningfully test its promises.

sections.title: Suffering, Divine Hiddenness, and the Design of Judgment
sections.rationale: The moral and explanatory adequacy of the gospel also turns on whether a fallen world, divine absence, severe suffering, and ultimate punishment fit a wise and just salvific plan.

routes.description: Establish a sufficiently reliable historical core of Jesus' death, the empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that a bodily resurrection explains that combined evidence within a relevant theistic background framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are adequately supported, the appearances are properly interpreted as bodily encounters, competing explanations lack comparable cumulative scope, and resurrection is rationally admissible given the relevant background evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical facts and comparative explanation to the conclusion that Jesus' bodily resurrection is rational.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early and sufficiently reliable source basis for the death, empty tomb, and reported appearances.
Show that the reported experiences and relevant texts concern bodily encounters rather than solely disembodied or private experiences.
Show that resurrection accounts for the combined evidence without requiring the unsupported conjunctions attributed to rival explanations.
Supply relevant background grounds under which resurrection is not excluded solely by ordinary expectations about death.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support actual death and an empty burial place as constraints on survival, vision-only, and body-removal accounts.
Use cumulative theistic or postmortem-awareness considerations only insofar as they bear on the antecedent plausibility of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and incomplete historical record underdetermines what occurred, that nonphysical experiences or unknown body-removal scenarios remain available, and that a miracle conclusion requires background commitments not established by the reports alone.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence cannot securely establish a publicly observable risen body, ordinary or unresolved alternatives remain live, or the prior theological requirements for identifying the event as divine resurrection are not independently warranted.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential underdetermination and the demanding miracle standard to withholding a bodily-resurrection conclusion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that source dates, partisanship, eyewitness status, and limited independent corroboration restrict the warranted historical inference.
Preserve a reasonable interpretation of the reported experiences that does not establish tangible, publicly observable bodily encounters.
Show that psychological experiences, unknown removal scenarios, or other unresolved possibilities prevent a unique resurrection inference.
Require justified beliefs about a supernatural agent and its intentions before identifying an extraordinary report as a resurrection miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether touching narratives and Pauline spiritual-body language actually establish bodily continuity and physical interaction.
Apply an evidential threshold appropriate to extraordinary perception and postmortem-awareness reports used to alter prior probability.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Testimony
sections.rationale: The reliability, dating, independence, and eyewitness connections of the surviving testimony determine what historical premises may enter either side's inference.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the condition of the burial place constrain survival, vision-only, body-removal, and resurrection accounts without alone deciding among them.

sections.title: Bodily Character of the Reported Appearances
sections.rationale: The motion specifically concerns bodily resurrection, making physical contact, group observation, Pauline terminology, and public corroboration a distinct burden-bearing issue.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether grief visions, conversion phenomena, collective experiences, removal scenarios, or combinations of them explain the historical claims.

sections.title: Prior Probability and the Miracle Framework
sections.rationale: The rationality of accepting an extraordinary conclusion depends partly on how natural-law expectations, theistic background beliefs, and alleged postmortem evidence bear on prior plausibility.

routes.description: Establish that a beginningless temporal sequence is excluded either because concrete actual infinities are metaphysically impossible or because a temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition, while answering challenges based on temporal symmetry, tense, quantifier scope, and paradox reformulations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one independent philosophical argument supplies adequate grounds for a finite past and its indispensable premises remain applicable to temporal reality after the principal infinity, symmetry, and traversal objections are addressed.

motionBridge.description: Connect a defensible prohibition on a beginningless temporal sequence to adequate philosophical support for the claim that the universe began to exist.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the properties illustrated by concrete actual-infinity cases warrant excluding an actually infinite collection of past events.
Supply a principled difference between an instantiated beginningless past and an endless future that preserves the finite-past inference.
Establish that temporal accumulation cannot produce or traverse an actual infinite merely because every particular finite member is reachable.
Show that reverse-counting, Grim Reaper, Hilbert-style, or causal-finitist reasoning independently excludes a beginningless temporal or causal sequence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the modal, tense, and distributive-versus-collective distinctions required by the central infinity arguments.
Explain why a beginningless process terminating at one finite point requires a non-arbitrary account of that endpoint.

routes.description: Withhold adequacy from the finite-past case by showing that counterintuitive infinite-set behavior does not establish impossibility, that past-future asymmetry is unsupported, and that successive-addition arguments conflate completion with memberwise coverage or rely on unresolved explanatory assumptions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal actual-infinity and successive-addition arguments each retain an indispensable unsupported inference, equivocation, or symmetry problem, without requiring an independent demonstration that the universe is beginningless.

motionBridge.description: Show that the offered infinity arguments do not adequately establish a beginning of the universe, while bearing no burden to prove a beginningless universe.

centralBridges.description: Require a justified inference from unusual Cantorian consequences to metaphysical impossibility rather than treating counterintuitiveness as sufficient.
Show that the treatment of a beginningless past and endless future requires an independently defensible temporal symmetry breaker.
Distinguish every member being reached from a completed terminal act and require proof that the disputed every-to-all inference fails in the relevant case.
Challenge the sufficiency, endpoint-explanation, accumulation, or possibility premises used by reverse-counting and paradox-based finite-past arguments.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Keep simple-future, future-perfect, past, and present-existence claims aligned when testing purported temporal asymmetries.
Maintain the distinction between undermining the offered support for a beginning and affirmatively establishing a beginningless past.

sections.title: Actual Infinity: From Cantorian Consequences to Metaphysical Impossibility
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal premise of the actual-infinity argument: whether Hilbert-style and related consequences justify excluding concrete actual infinities, or merely display familiar features of infinite collections.

sections.title: Past–Future Parity, Temporal Becoming, and Tense
sections.rationale: The finite-past inference depends on whether elapsed past events and unrealized future events differ in a way that blocks temporal mirroring without equivocating among present, future, and future-perfect claims.

sections.title: Successive Addition, Endless Counting, and Quantifier Scope
sections.rationale: This section contains the main clash over whether temporal succession can encompass every member of an infinite series, and whether memberwise reachability entails a collectively completed actual infinite.

sections.title: Beginningless Countdowns, Completion, and Endpoint Explanation
sections.rationale: Reverse-counting cases test whether infinitely much prior activity is sufficient for completion and whether a modest explanatory principle can exclude an otherwise arbitrary finishing point.

sections.title: Grim Reapers, Hilbert Reformulations, and Causal Finitism
sections.rationale: Alternative paradox and causal formulations matter because they may provide an independent finite-past route, but their force depends on possibility, accumulation, temporal-mirroring, and causal-structure premises.

routes.description: Establish Christian belief as an intellectually responsible interpretation of reality and as a morally constructive tradition whose central resources support meaning, transformation, forgiveness, and resistance to dehumanizing violence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a defensible account of religious inference under evidential uncertainty, explains how Christianity contributes meaning and moral orientation, and distinguishes its governing norms from pathological or extremist uses of religion.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christian belief can remain intellectually credible in the modern world while its governing commitments can make a constructive moral contribution.

centralBridges.description: Explain why scientific accounts do not exhaust questions of existence, meaning, and value, and why religious belief may function as a challengeable inference rather than privileged certainty.
Identify Christian resources for transformation, forgiveness, human dignity, and restraint of violence that connect the tradition's central claims to constructive conduct.
Show why coercion and violence should not be attributed uniquely or necessarily to religion, while providing a principled basis for criticizing religious abuses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Give morally coherent interpretations of resurrection, redemption, and scriptural development sufficient to answer objections grounded in sacrifice, punishment, or violent texts.
Establish that psychological desire cannot by itself determine whether religious or nonreligious belief is true.

routes.description: Establish that specific religious claims lack adequate evidential support, that morality and solidarity do not require supernatural authority, and that central doctrines and authoritative texts create distinctive mechanisms of submission, coercion, and harm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it undermines the evidential warrant for revealed religion, provides a viable secular basis for ethical life, and connects religious authority or doctrine to harms that cannot be dismissed solely as accidental fringe distortions.

motionBridge.description: Show that modern religious belief is evidentially unsupported and that its authoritative structures or doctrines produce morally significant risks of coercion and harm.

centralBridges.description: Use scientific history, cosmology, and epistemic limits to challenge human-centered creation and detailed claims about divine intentions, revelation, miracles, or salvation.
Ground moral discrimination, reciprocity, and solidarity in human capacities and social development without dependence on divine commands or supernatural premises.
Connect scriptural or divine authority to compelled belief, violent commands, punishment, and conduct that independent moral judgment would otherwise reject.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether redemption, sacrifice, original sin, and hell can be reconciled with personal responsibility and genuinely voluntary acceptance.
Answer comparisons with secular totalitarianism by distinguishing the con burden from any claim that nonreligious ideologies are incapable of violence.

sections.title: Scientific Explanation, Religious Inference, and Epistemic Credibility
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether modern cosmology, evolution, and scientific explanation displace religious claims or leave room for a public, fallible religious interpretation of existence, meaning, and value.

sections.title: Moral Foundations, Obligation, and Human Solidarity
sections.rationale: The motion's constructive-morality dimension requires comparison between transcendent accounts of obligation and secular accounts grounded in moral discrimination, reciprocity, evolved sociality, and solidarity.

sections.title: Religious Authority, Violence, and Moral Restraint
sections.rationale: This section tests whether violence is intrinsic to authoritative religious commitments or better explained by extremist capture, and whether Christian interpretive and ethical resources can constrain coercion and dehumanization.

sections.title: Redemption, Sacrifice, Punishment, and Freedom
sections.rationale: Christianity's moral credibility substantially depends on whether sacrifice and salvation can be understood as freely accepted transformation or instead entail transferred responsibility, threatened punishment, and coercive submission.

sections.title: Consolation, Meaning, and Human Flourishing
sections.rationale: The debate also turns on whether religion's promises of consolation and meaning compromise truth-seeking or can coexist with intellectual responsibility while contributing to well-being, hope, and constructive personal orientation.

routes.description: Establish historical credibility for bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity through early Pauline testimony, substantively stable textual transmission, external identification of early Christian belief, and persistence of apostolic church structures and doctrines.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Paul warrants a bodily-resurrection reading, transmission and hostile-witness evidence reliably identify early Christian belief, and institutional and doctrinal continuities connect the first-century church with later Catholic and related apostolic communions.

motionBridge.description: Connect the Pauline, transmission, hostile-witness, and church-structure evidence to the historical credibility of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the early undisputed Pauline letters attest a real bodily resurrection and a risen-Christ appearance rather than merely an immaterial vision.
Establish that manuscript stability and external testimony preserve and independently identify an early, historically rooted Christian belief tradition.
Trace first-century leadership offices and essential doctrines through the pre-Nicene period and later apostolic communions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Roman, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac differences coexist with substantial agreement on essential doctrines, councils, and apostolic orders.
Distinguish reforms that retained inherited Catholic doctrine from later movements that discarded it when characterizing historical continuity.

routes.description: Deny that the cited materials establish bodily resurrection or a uniquely Catholic lineage by emphasizing visionary and secondhand alternatives for Paul, uncertainty in transmission and preservation, early Christian diversity, and context-dependent religious branching.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline reports remain compatible with visionary or inherited interpretations, surviving sources cannot securely overcome transmission and selection uncertainty, or early diversity and later branching prevent identification of one continuous Catholic institution.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence named in the motion remains insufficient to make bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity historically credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and witness traditions do not establish a bodily encounter or independently prove an earlier resurrection event.
Show that copying gaps, oral and written transmission, authorial selection, and selective survival limit the evidential force of Christian and hostile sources.
Show that competing early groups, divergent regional churches, and conciliar formation complicate identification of a uniquely continuous Catholic orthodoxy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the continuity case to distinguish the existence of a small pre-Constantinian group from widespread or uniquely authoritative orthodoxy.
Use earlier reform movements and shared Christian scripture and history to test claims that later divisions constitute categorical religious rupture.

sections.title: Pauline evidence and bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: The earliest Pauline material is central to whether the resurrection claim concerns a tangible risen body and whether Paul's reported experience and inherited witness list provide independent historical support.

sections.title: Textual stability and Gospel transmission
sections.rationale: Historical use of Christian writings depends on distinguishing substantive manuscript stability from uncertainty about earlier sources, interpolations, transmission across decades, and authorial selection.

sections.title: Hostile witnesses and preservation effects
sections.rationale: External descriptions may help identify early Christian beliefs, but their force depends on whether surviving hostile materials independently represent the period or reflect selective preservation.

sections.title: Early orthodoxy and institutional continuity
sections.rationale: The Catholic-continuity burden turns on whether first-century leadership structures persist through the pre-Nicene era despite a small population, competing groups, councils, and uncertainty about early development.

sections.title: Apostolic communions, reform, and religious branching
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, and Protestant traditions test whether shared doctrine, councils, orders, scripture, and history demonstrate continuity or instead support multiple context-dependent Christian branches.

routes.description: Establish that Iraq's conduct justified regime removal under a defensible intervention principle and that human reason and solidarity provide moral guidance without divine authority, while religious doctrines can corrupt judgment and political conduct.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the intervention is connected to sufficient humanitarian and security grounds and material consequences, and if secular moral agency is shown adequate while claimed divine authority is shown epistemically unnecessary or capable of licensing harmful conduct.

motionBridge.description: Connect a justified exception to Iraqi sovereignty with an account of moral authority grounded independently of religion and vulnerable to corruption by divine claims.

centralBridges.description: Specify the atrocities, aggression, proliferation concerns, or other conditions under which Iraq could forfeit protection against intervention.
Show that the consequences of removing the regime materially support the claimed humanitarian and security justification despite acknowledged costs.
Explain how objective inquiry, human solidarity, or reciprocal interests can sustain moral judgment without supernatural command.
Demonstrate how particular doctrines or assertions of divine permission can undermine autonomy, excuse cruelty, or obstruct peaceful political judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the secular account by distinguishing unresolved natural questions from evidence for a personal moral lawgiver.
Distinguish secular humanism from political systems whose violence cannot be attributed to unbelief alone.

routes.description: Establish that the Iraq invasion lacked a coherent and prudent justification once its foreseeable harms and selective doctrine are considered, and that transcendent moral authority supplies obligations and restraints that secular accounts cannot adequately ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if war is shown to require a burden not met by claimed intentions or benefits, and if religious belief is connected to objective obligation, moral formation, or civilizational restraint while major claims of uniquely religious corruption are answered.

motionBridge.description: Connect the presumption against aggressive war with the need for a transcendent source of binding moral obligation and social restraint.

centralBridges.description: Require a coherent principle and sufficiently compelling necessity before the harms of aggressive intervention can be morally authorized.
Account for civilian, strategic, institutional, and geopolitical costs when determining whether the Iraq invasion was defensible.
Explain why moral knowledge, solidarity, or self-interest alone may not create objective duties or secure obedience to them.
Show how religious narratives, atonement, hope, and transcendent accountability can redirect destructive impulses and sustain moral order.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use experience with failed interventions and selective applications to test confidence in humanitarian-war reasoning.
Test claims about secular moral sufficiency against revolutionary or state persecution explicitly hostile to religion.

sections.title: Iraq: Necessity, Aggression, and Sovereignty
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether Saddam Hussein's conduct crossed a defensible threshold for intervention or whether initiating war remained an unjustified act despite the character of the regime.

sections.title: Iraq: Consequences and the Consistency of Intervention
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of benefits, human and strategic costs, nonproliferation effects, and selective enforcement are necessary to connect the intervention principle to its practical application.

sections.title: Secular and Transcendent Foundations of Moral Authority
sections.rationale: This is the principal clash over whether solidarity, reason, and reciprocal interest can ground binding moral duties or whether objective obligation requires authority beyond humanity.

sections.title: Religious Doctrine: Corruption or Moral Formation
sections.rationale: Disputes over sacrifice, atonement, punishment, divine permission, and religious experience test whether characteristic doctrines cultivate restraint and hope or compromise autonomous moral judgment.

sections.title: Reason, Historical Violence, and Social Consequences
sections.rationale: Scientific explanation and rival interpretations of atheist and religious political violence provide material tests of the broader causal claims linking belief or unbelief to civilization and harm.

routes.description: Establish a mind-first account in which irreducible consciousness, religious and moral experience, and meaningful agency jointly make better sense if reality has a conscious, purposive, intelligent divine ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these features resist an exclusively material or evolutionary account, receive a coherent unified explanation from a divine ground, and warrant the motion-level inference to God rather than merely identifying unresolved mysteries.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative mind-first explanation of consciousness, experience, morality, and agency to the existence of a conscious, purposive divine ground.

centralBridges.description: Establish that conscious experience is epistemically prior and ontologically irreducible rather than exhaustively explicable as neural activity.
Show why consciousness as a basic feature of reality supports a necessary mind-like ground of the universe.
Establish that religious experience can provide rational access to transcendent reality despite interpretive diversity and evolutionary explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why binding moral commitment requires more than a genetic or socially useful disposition.
Support a conception of persons and agency not exhausted by deterministic physical causation.

routes.description: Maintain that naturalistic accounts can absorb consciousness, religious and moral experience, and meaningful agency while unresolved explanatory gaps and shared mysteries do not uniquely support a divine reality.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if evolutionary, psychological, neural, and compatibilist explanations remain viable, the proposed theistic account adds no independently warranted explanation, and the shared evidence underdetermines the motion's inference to God.

motionBridge.description: Show that the acknowledged phenomena and mysteries permit competing interpretations and therefore do not warrant the motion-level conclusion that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish an unresolved mind-body problem from positive evidence for theism and require explanatory gain from invoking God.
Account for religious and moral experience through evolved psychological and social dispositions without requiring divine foundations.
Establish that compatibilist freedom can preserve meaningful human agency within causal determination.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use evidential limits on mentality without brain activity to constrain claims about disembodied consciousness and survival.
Show that idealist or theological interpretation must distinguish reality from imagination and outperform alternative paradigms.

sections.title: Consciousness and the mind-body explanatory gap
sections.rationale: The debate's primary clash concerns whether consciousness is epistemically and ontologically basic, reducible to brain processes, or an unresolved phenomenon that supports neither ontology by itself.

sections.title: From mind-first reality to a divine ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests the indispensable motion bridge from the fundamentality of consciousness or idealism to a necessary conscious, purposive, intelligent ground identified as God.

sections.title: Disembodied consciousness and personal continuity
sections.rationale: Near-death reports, brain dependence, logical possibility, and alternative embodiment bear on whether consciousness and personal identity can exist independently of present physical brains.

sections.title: Religious experience and naturalistic explanation
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must address whether transformative and cross-cultural religious experiences disclose transcendent reality or arise from variable evolved psychological dispositions.

sections.title: Moral experience and objective grounding
sections.rationale: The issue determines whether practical moral commitment requires an objective divine basis or can remain meaningful and usable as an evolved social phenomenon.

sections.title: Free agency and causal determination
sections.rationale: The agency branch of the motion turns on whether meaningful freedom requires an escape from physical causation or can be preserved through a naturalistic compatibilist account.

routes.description: Establish that a personal transcendent ground provides a unified explanation for the origin and order of nature, rational inquiry, biological information, objective morality, and the possibility of evil.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these features require or are better unified by an intelligent, immaterial, morally sufficient ground and if objections from natural alternatives, moral relativity, and suffering do not defeat that comparison.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative explanatory inferences to theism as a more adequate account of reality than atheism.

centralBridges.description: Infer a transcendent intelligent cause from cosmic beginning, fine-tuning, and purposive order.
Ground trustworthy reason, scientific inquiry, and specified biological information in an immaterial intelligence.
Show that objective moral duties and human rights require a standard beyond individual or social preference.
Reconcile suffering with divine goodness through freedom, limited human knowledge, and the possibility of wider goods or justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish positive and potentially falsifiable design inference from an appeal based only on current ignorance.
Derive the relevant divine attributes from the kinds of effects the cumulative case seeks to explain.

routes.description: Establish that revisable natural inquiry and human responsibility explain or responsibly address reality without positing God, while testing theistic inferences against alternative accounts, contrary evidence, and suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed divine explanation lacks sufficient evidential support or explanatory necessity, natural and social accounts remain viable, and the attributes assigned to God generate unresolved tensions with observed reality.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential restraint, natural inquiry, and human responsibility to atheism as the better comparative approach to reality.

centralBridges.description: Show that unknown origins, observer selection, and inhospitable conditions do not warrant a transcendent designer.
Use cumulative evolution and established natural history as alternatives to sudden design and disputed creation accounts.
Account for moral judgment, empathy, and responsibility through human social life without an objective divine lawgiver.
Test omnipotence, foreknowledge, and benevolence against severe suffering and the claimed consequences of created freedom.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require independent evidence before treating an unexplained phenomenon as support for a law-transcending deity.
Assess whether scriptural moral and historical claims support the explanatory authority attributed to theism.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Fine-Tuning, and Design
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal inference from the universe's beginning and apparent order to a transcendent intelligence against uncertainty, observer selection, and evidence of inhospitable or imperfect conditions.

sections.title: Reason, Knowledge, and Scientific Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether rational and scientific practice requires an immaterial theistic foundation or can proceed through evidential restraint, revisability, and natural inquiry without that grounding.

sections.title: Biological Information, Evolution, and Natural History
sections.rationale: This issue compares intelligent-cause inferences from biological information with cumulative evolutionary explanation and examines how established natural history bears on creation claims.

sections.title: Morality, Empathy, and Human Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether binding moral standards require a transcendent ground or whether social judgment, evolved empathy, and accountable human choice provide the relevant atheistic account.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, Freedom, and Divine Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether severe suffering is compatible with an omnipotent, omniscient, benevolent God and whether freedom, foreknowledge distinctions, wider goods, or human limits answer that challenge.

routes.description: Establish that the defended doctrine concerns freely maintained separation and sin's internal consequences, while divine grace, corrective sanctification, and possible annihilation prevent hell from being externally imposed endless torture.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if culpable persistence after adequate disclosure can ground exile, suffering functions as a consequence or restorative process rather than arbitrary torture, rescue remains genuinely available, and final destruction limits otherwise endless suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that self-chosen exile, sanctifying grace, and possible annihilation jointly provide a morally coherent Christian account of hell distinct from external torture.

centralBridges.description: Establish that informed attachment to pride or self-rule can constitute a responsible refusal of reconciliation rather than mere involuntary disbelief.
Explain infernal suffering as internally developing corruption or painful restoration, with grace available to any soul that genuinely seeks reconciliation.
Account for duration and proportionality by allowing release through transformation, universal reconciliation, or the eventual dissolution of a persistently alienated finite soul.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require adequate information and a fair opportunity for correction so honest confusion is distinguished from persistent informed rejection.
Connect death, exile, final justice, and Christ-mediated rescue to the broader theological framework that gives the proposed alternatives their moral function.

routes.description: Establish that apparent rejection of God is shaped by involuntary belief, misleading information, psychological incapacity, and arbitrary circumstances, so suffering or destruction cannot be justified by calling the resulting separation self-chosen.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the required refusal is not adequately informed and voluntary, if grace and full disclosure instead imply eventual reconciliation, or if the duration, suffering, annihilation, and rescue framework remains disproportionate or internally incoherent.

motionBridge.description: Show that relabeling hell as exile, sanctification, or annihilation does not morally justify its suffering or finality without informed agency, proportionality, and coherent rescue conditions.

centralBridges.description: Establish that belief and apparent rejection arise from evidence, upbringing, psychology, or hiddenness rather than a freely selected preference for separation.
Show that occupants either cannot escape, misunderstand their options, or would seek available grace once informed, undermining continued exile as a voluntary condition.
Test whether finite wrongdoing can justify prolonged suffering or annihilation and whether the theological account of death, exile, and substitution consistently bears that burden.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require a fair opportunity for postmortem clarification and change rather than allowing death or contingent religious circumstances to fix a person's fate.
Determine whether complete information, divine mercy, and universally available grace leave any coherent basis for permanent non-reconciliation.

sections.title: Self-Chosen Exile and Internal Consequences
sections.rationale: This issue defines the proposed alternative to external torture and tests whether pride, self-rule, and progressive moral corruption can make separation and its suffering genuinely attributable to the person.

sections.title: Epistemic Agency, Hiddenness, and Fair Opportunity
sections.rationale: The moral status of exile depends on whether rejection can remain responsible despite involuntary belief formation, motivated reasoning, misinformation, divine hiddenness, and the contingency of death.

sections.title: Sanctifying Grace, Escape, and Universalism
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether painful transformation and available divine assistance make hell escapable, whether incapacity or defective preference defeats voluntariness, and whether the stated rescue conditions imply universal reconciliation.

sections.title: Duration, Proportionality, and Possible Annihilation
sections.rationale: The justification must address the relation between finite wrongdoing and potentially prolonged suffering while determining whether eventual dissolution, continued sin, or release supplies a proportionate final outcome.

sections.title: Final Justice, Death, Exile, and Atonement
sections.rationale: The broader account of divine justice and Christ-mediated rescue bears on what consequence sin incurs, how death or exile is overcome, and whether the proposed hell model fits its theological mechanism of reconciliation.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative theistic explanation from cosmic origin and order, biological information, rational consciousness, objective morality, scientific regularity, and historically grounded religious claims.
routes.successCriteria: Show that these features jointly require or are better accounted for by an immaterial, intelligent, personal, and morally authoritative creator, while answering naturalistic alternatives and the principal objections from evil and religious uncertainty.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative case to the conclusion that theism explains the disputed features of reality more adequately than skeptical naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Derive a transcendent and causally adequate ground from the beginning, contingency, and ordered conditions of material reality.
Establish that biological information and nature's lawlike, goal-directed order require an intelligent source beyond unguided physical processes.
Establish that trustworthy rational thought and meaningful agency require grounding in a rational mind rather than wholly determined material reactions.
Establish that objective moral value, evil, and ultimate justice require a standard grounded beyond human attitudes and social development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve the theistic inference by answering objections from suffering, apparent imperfection, cosmic timing, and competing natural histories.
Supply publicly relevant historical grounds for moving from generic theism toward Christianity through the resurrection claim.

routes.description: Defend skeptical naturalism through evidential restraint, scientific explanation, emergent accounts of mind and morality, and objections to the explanatory sufficiency and expected consequences of theism.
routes.successCriteria: Show that theistic conclusions outrun the available evidence, that naturalistic mechanisms or open inquiry address the disputed phenomena without divine agency, and that suffering, imperfection, religious diversity, and weak miracle evidence reduce theism's comparative adequacy.

motionBridge.description: Connect scientific inquiry and evidential restraint to the conclusion that skeptical naturalism is the better-supported approach to explaining reality.

centralBridges.description: Require publicly assessable evidence, possible disconfirmation, and explanatory mechanisms before accepting supernatural causal claims.
Provide naturalistic accounts of biological development, rational agency, morality, purpose, and improbable events without invoking divine agency.
Show that cosmic origins and unresolved explanatory gaps do not uniquely establish a finite beginning, a transcendent cause, or the Christian God.
Show that suffering, apparent imperfection, cosmic timing, and religious nonconvergence conflict with expectations generated by the proposed God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Contrast science's organized error correction and convergence with faith-based methods and incompatible religious conclusions.
Apply evidential, probabilistic, and selection-bias considerations to resurrection, miracle, and providence claims.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Contingency, and Order
sections.rationale: Covers whether the universe's beginning, material composition, initial conditions, and regularity require a transcendent intelligent cause or remain open to natural histories and competing possibilities.

sections.title: Biological Information and Evolutionary Explanation
sections.rationale: Addresses whether genetic information and the first replicating system indicate intelligent agency or whether evolutionary mechanisms and physical conditions adequately explain biological complexity.

sections.title: Reason, Consciousness, and Agency
sections.rationale: Tests whether material naturalism can ground trustworthy reasoning and volition or whether these capacities require a rational, nonmaterial source.

sections.title: Morality, Evil, and Justice
sections.rationale: Encompasses the dispute over objective moral grounding, secular accounts based on harm and reciprocity, the evidential problem of suffering, and claims about ultimate justice.

sections.title: Evidence, Science, and Explanatory Method
sections.rationale: Examines burdens of belief, falsifiability, explanatory gaps, scientific correction, and whether invoking God supplies an adequate causal explanation of reality.

sections.title: Religious Diversity and Resurrection Evidence
sections.rationale: Addresses whether incompatible religions and personal faith undermine specific Christian claims or whether cumulative and historical resurrection evidence distinguishes Christianity.
